text: Bacteria live in and on almost every material and environment; only a small number of the thousands of bacterial species are pathogenic (disease-causing) — for example, the billions of bacteria in a cow's rumen are essential for nutrition rather than harmful. A bacterium is a single cell, about 0.001 mm in size (roughly 3,000 times bigger than a virus) and visible with an ordinary optical microscope. Bacterial cells come in three main shapes — spherical (cocci), rod-shaped (bacilli), and spiral — and share a basic structure: a cell wall/capsule for protection and shape, a water-based cytoplasm holding nutrient stores, floating genetic material (DNA), a flagella (tail) for movement, and pili (hair-like structures) for attaching to organs. Like other cells, bacteria need energy, nitrogen, and carbon sources (organic matter in litter, dead animals, or rubbish can supply these), plus water, trace elements, and sometimes oxygen. Bacteria reproduce by fission — the cell grows, duplicates its DNA, and splits into two identical daughter cells — at very high speed: E. coli can divide every 20 minutes, so 10 bacteria can become more than 600 billion after 12 hours under good conditions, even though many die off as the animal's body fights back. This rapid multiplication is why treatment for E. coli-caused diarrhea must start as early as possible. All animals are constantly exposed to bacteria on their body surfaces (skin, gut, lungs) through air, water, soil, and feed, and most are normally harmless thanks to the animal's natural defenses. Infection is like a miniature battle between bacteria and the animal's defenses, and it takes hold when natural defenses are weak (stress, fatigue, parasites, other disease), when bacterial numbers in the environment are very high (e.g. many sick animals shedding bacteria in a group), or when the bacteria are especially aggressive (highly pathogenic). Bacterial disease develops once bacteria enter the body, attach to organs, multiply heavily, and reach the bloodstream.
